card.summary: A 1‑storey, 4‑room colonial bungalow with white shingled walls, hardwood floors, and classic detailing, sized 792 cm × 1417 cm × 300 cm.
card.description: The Desoto colonial bungalow presents a dignified yet modest streetscape, its white shingled walls rising 300 cm from a solid concrete slab to a gently sloped asphalt‑shingled roof. Measuring 792 cm wide by 1417 cm deep, the single‑storey volume is organized into four well‑proportioned rooms: a welcoming living area, two private bedrooms, and a full bathroom, each framed by timber joists and finished with hardwood flooring and crisp white paint. The front entry is marked by a solid wood door on sturdy hinges, while a sliding aluminum door opens onto the rear, inviting natural light through eight double‑glazed windows that punctuate the façade. Interior partitions of gypsum board define spaces without sacrificing the open, airy feel typical of 1920s pattern‑book homes. Classic colonial details such as symmetrical window placement, modest cornice trim, and a modest front stoop (absent here but implied by the style) give the house a timeless character. Modern comforts are discreetly integrated: an electrical service panel, HVAC ductwork, and a modest thermostat ensure contemporary livability while preserving the historic aesthetic. Every element—from the shingled roof to the hardwood floor—fits within the overall envelope, respecting the proportion that the original pattern‑book intended, and the house stands ready for occupation after a final inspection.
plan: Measure the lot and stake out a 792 cm by 1417 cm rectangle to confirm clearances and grading.
Draft a full‑scale site plan and architectural elevations, confirming a single‑storey colonial bungalow with a 300 cm overall height.
Excavate, pour a reinforced concrete slab foundation, and install floor joists and subfloor sheathing.
Erect exterior wood‑siding walls, install interior gypsum partitions, and frame the roof truss system.
Apply asphalt shingles, install doors, windows, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and finish interior finishes such as hardwood flooring and paint.
Conduct a final inspection, test all operable components, and hand over the completed home to the owner.
assumptions: The interior wall finish is assumed to be gypsum board painted white, a common choice for 1920s bungalow interiors.
HVAC is provided as a single‑zone forced‑air system, typical for a modest single‑storey home of this era.
Plumbing fixtures are assumed to be standard chrome fixtures with a bathtub, sink, and toilet in the single bathroom.
No garage or porch is included because the brief did not specify them; a detached carport could be added later if desired.

Do you prefer any specific interior colour palette beyond the default white walls, such as accent colours for the living room or bedrooms?
Is there a requirement for any additional utility spaces, such as a laundry room or pantry, that were not mentioned in the brief?

card.summary: A two‑storey Georgian‑style home of 13.26 m × 9.75 m with a front porch, sun parlor, three bedrooms, one bathroom, and a big blue couch placed on the porch.
card.description: The residence follows the classic 1920s Deboer pattern‑book design, presenting a dignified two‑storey Georgian façade that measures 1326 cm wide by 975 cm deep. A raised concrete slab foundation supports sturdy 2×6 lumber wall framing, topped by engineered roof trusses sheathed in OSB and finished with dark grey asphalt shingles. The front elevation is anchored by a welcoming porch of composite decking, its sloped roof echoing the main roofline and providing a sheltered space for a striking big blue couch that invites neighbours to linger. Inside, the ground floor offers a spacious living room, a kitchen with oak cabinets, a sun parlor flooded with double‑hung windows, and a full bathroom; the second floor houses three well‑proportioned bedrooms, each accessed by a graceful carpeted staircase. Light grey interior paint and oak hardwood floors create a timeless palette, while fiber‑cement siding and traditional wooden doors reinforce the house’s historic character. Modern comforts are discreetly integrated through concealed plumbing, electrical, and HVAC systems, ensuring the home reads as both a nostalgic homage and a functional contemporary dwelling.
plan: Measure the lot at 1326 cm by 975 cm and confirm setbacks, utility connections, and grading requirements.
Draft full‑scale architectural drawings based on the Deboer pattern‑book plan, allocating three bedrooms, one bathroom, a kitchen/dining, a sun parlor and a front porch within the 2‑storey envelope.
Submit the drawings for building permits, then order structural lumber, concrete, asphalt shingles, double‑hung windows, exterior doors and interior finish materials.
Excavate to a depth of 30 cm, install perimeter footings, and pour a 20 cm thick reinforced concrete slab foundation sized 1326 cm × 975 cm.
Erect the wood frame for ground‑floor walls, floor joists, second‑floor joists, and roof trusses, then install windows, exterior doors, and the main staircase.
Run plumbing, electrical, and HVAC rough‑ins, then seal walls and roof with insulation and vapor barrier.
Apply drywall, tape, and finish with a light grey paint on interior walls, and install hardwood flooring throughout the living areas.
Cover the roof with asphalt shingles, attach the front porch deck and its sloped roof, and finish the porch with a durable composite railing.
Place interior furnishings, positioning the big blue couch on the front porch to create an inviting outdoor seating area.
Perform a final inspection, verify all systems operate, and hand over the completed residence to the owner.
assumptions: Because the brief did not specify a garage, the design includes no garage structure.
Standard 2‑car driveway width of 600 cm is assumed to be provided on the property but not modeled as part of the house.
The interior finish palette is assumed to be light grey paint on walls and oak hardwood flooring, typical of 1920s pattern‑book homes.
Utility connections (water, sewer, electricity) are assumed to be available at the street front and are routed through the foundation slab.
questions: Do you prefer the big blue couch to be placed on the front porch or inside the living room?
Would you like a garage added, and if so, what size (e.g., 2‑car) and location?
What orientation of the house on the lot (north‑facing front, east‑facing front, etc.) would you like for optimal sunlight in the sun parlor?

card.name: A single‑storey, white‑brick home of 1325
card.summary: A single‑storey, white‑brick home of 1325 cm × 975 cm, 300 cm tall, with a blue couch in the living‑room and classic colonial details.
card.description: The residence presents a dignified brick façade painted in crisp white, its 1325 cm by 975 cm footprint anchored by a reinforced‑concrete slab. A single‑storey volume rises to a modest 300 cm, capped with asphalt‑shingle roofing that slopes gently toward a modest gable, punctuated by a central skylight illuminating the sun‑parlor. The front elevation is balanced by a centered solid‑wood entry door, flanked by double‑hung aluminum‑frame windows that echo the colonial rhythm of the original pattern‑book. A two‑car garage occupies the left wing, its steel‑panel door sliding silently. A welcoming porch stretches across the façade, finished in pressure‑treated decking and topped with a metal railing. Inside, the layout follows a classic plan: a spacious living‑room hosts a big blue couch (250 cm × 100 cm × 90 cm) centered before two pendant lamps, while the adjacent kitchen offers twelve cabinets of laminated plywood. Three bedrooms, two full bathrooms with ceramic tile, and a sun‑parlor with skylight complete the functional core. All interior walls are brick‑faced with drywall finishes, and hardwood flooring runs throughout the main living areas, providing a warm, cohesive aesthetic that honors the 1920s pattern‑book while meeting modern comfort.
plan: Measure the lot dimensions and verify the 1325 cm by 975 cm footprint against zoning setbacks.
Draft a scaled 2‑D plan showing foundation walls, interior partitions, and the location of the living room, kitchen, bedrooms, bathrooms, sun parlor and porch.
Create a 3‑D BIM model in Revit at LOD 200, extruding walls to a 274 cm ceiling height and adding roof geometry to reach a total height of 300 cm.
Coordinate with structural, electrical and plumbing trades to embed rebar, conduit and pipe schedules into the model.
Fabricate and install the concrete slab, brick veneer walls, roof trusses, windows, doors and interior finishes according to the BIM‑generated shop drawings.
Place the big blue couch in the living‑room, connect lighting, perform a final inspection and hand over the completed home.
assumptions: The brief did not specify the number of bedrooms or bathrooms, so a typical three‑bedroom, two‑bath layout was chosen.
Wall material was not given; brick was selected to match the colonial style of the reference designs.
Roof material was inferred from the Carlton reference and set to asphalt shingles.
A two‑car garage and a front porch were assumed because most 1920s pattern‑book homes included these features.
questions: Should the blue couch be positioned against a specific wall or centered in the living‑room?
Do you prefer any particular interior finish colour for the walls or flooring beyond the default white and oak?
Will you require any additional specialty rooms such as a home office or laundry space?
